summary: Defines Augmented BNF, a compact notation for writing the syntax of protocols and message formats. It separates this definition out of the early email specifications so that others can cite it, with some changes and additions. It was replaced by RFC 4234.

plainLanguage.summary: ABNF is a grammar notation that lets people write down exactly what a protocol message must look like. RFC 2234 standardises that notation so it can be cited by many specs.

questions: how to write protocol syntax rules
how do abnf repetition operators work
what is the difference between abnf and bnf
subtitle: A compact notation for writing down the exact syntax of protocol messages.

tldr.problem: Internet specifications each had their own variant of syntax notation, making them hard to reference consistently.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2234 pulls Augmented BNF (ABNF) into its own document with clear rules for naming, terminals, operators and repetition, and even defines ABNF in ABNF.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2234 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4234; new work should cite the newer version.

today: RFC 2234 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4234.

sections.title: Why ABNF Was Split Out
sections.content:
Augmented BNF (ABNF) is a compact notation for specifying the grammar of protocol messages. Earlier specs, including email specs like RFC 733 and RFC 822, each included their own copy. RFC 2234 separates it out so it can be referenced selectively and adds modifications.

ABNF differs from standard BNF in several ways: rule naming, repetition, alternatives, order-independence and value ranges.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of each rulebook redefining how to write its rules, this puts one standard set of rules for writing rules in a single place.

sections.title: Rules, Names and Terminal Values
sections.content:
A rule has the form name = elements crlf. Names start with an alphabetic character followed by letters, digits and hyphens; names are case-insensitive. Angle brackets may be used in prose to highlight a rule name.

Values are terminal characters (integers). They can be written with bases: b for binary, d for decimal, x for hexadecimal. For example CR = %d13 or %x0D. A dot joins values like CRLF = %d13.10.

Literal strings are quoted and are case-insensitive US-ASCII. To force exact case, each character must be given numerically. The wire encoding is not defined by ABNF itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule gives a name and a pattern. Characters can be written as numbers in different bases, or as quoted text which ignores case.

sections.title: Operators
sections.content:
Concatenation means elements appear in order. foo / bar means either. =/ adds alternatives to an existing rule. %x30-39 gives a numeric range.

Parentheses (...) group elements. Repetition *element means 0 or more; 1*element means at least 1; n*m element means n to m; 2DIGIT means exactly 2. [...] is optional (same as *1). A semicolon ; starts a comment to end of line.

Operator precedence (tightest to loosest): strings/names, comment, range, repetition, grouping/option, concatenation, alternative. The RFC recommends using parentheses to avoid ambiguity.
sections.plainLanguage: Slashes pick one option. Stars repeat. Brackets make things optional. Parentheses group things together. Comments start with semicolons.

sections.title: ABNF Defined in ABNF
sections.content:
Section 4 formally defines ABNF's own grammar in ABNF. A rulelist contains rules, blank lines or comments. A rule is a rulename, a defined-as (= or =/), its elements and a newline; continuation lines must start with whitespace.

The definition covers repeat, group, option, char-val, num-val (binary/decimal/hex), and prose-val (descriptive text in angle brackets as a last resort).
sections.plainLanguage: The notation is self-describing: the rules for ABNF are written using ABNF itself.

sections.title: Core Rules and Security
sections.content:
Appendix A lists core rules: ALPHA, BIT, CHAR, CR, LF, CRLF, DIGIT, DQUOTE, HEXDIG, HTAB, SP, VCHAR, WSP, OCTET, LWSP. These assume 7-bit US-ASCII in an 8-bit field with high bit zero, in network byte order.

Security considerations say security is not relevant to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Appendix A gives a standard set of basic building blocks (like letters, digits, spaces) for others to reuse.
